hypothesis: Dropping the expensive mobility term from the move-ordering estimate retains most of static evaluator ordering's alpha-beta node reduction while materially reducing ordering overhead and preserving Baseline A actions.
interpretation: Action equivalence held at every tested frozen position for depths 2, 3, and 4.
At depth 2 neither ordering strategy can improve pruning below the root. Score-only ordering remained 26.9 percent slower than baseline, though about 9.2 percent faster than full-static ordering.

At depth 3 score-only ordering exactly matched full-static ordering's 36.2 percent node reduction: 3776 baseline nodes fell to 2409. Removing mobility made it about 11.4 percent faster than full-static ordering, but it was still 65.6 percent slower than baseline overall.

At depth 4 score-only ordering reduced nodes by 44.0 percent, versus 46.6 percent for full-static ordering. It was about 8.3 percent faster than full-static ordering, but remained 17.0 percent slower than baseline.

The experiment supports the narrower hypothesis that mobility computation was a meaningful part of ordering overhead, but not the stronger hypothesis that score-only ordering is independently a runtime win.

The search tree remains strongly order-sensitive. The next clean experiment may add the already-validated structural exact transposition table to score-only ordering and measure its incremental effect; this changes one factor relative to the score-ordered engine while preserving evaluator and move-order policy.
